data.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: explorer inspires youth through glacial field trips
data.description:
When Wilson Cheung took Hong Kong secondary school students into the Swiss Alps this summer, terrain he had once been able to reach had become inaccessible.
Glacier melt and thawing ground had destabilised parts of the mountain, while rockfall made fieldwork more hazardous.
Only weeks earlier, Cheung had completed a roughly 1,700km (1,056-mile) scientific snowkite traverse across Greenland in 2026. The journey took him across the ice sheet while he continued collecting data in one of the world’s most extreme environments.
“We can see it in the measurements, but when we are actually there, we see the physical changes in front of you,” he said.
Cheung is a finalist for the Spirit of Perseverance Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
His route into glaciology was far from conventional.
Cheung grew up in a low-income family and struggled with English at school. With little money at home, his mother often sent him to the library, where the air-conditioning was free and there were plenty of books to read.
After graduating from Baptist University and struggling to find suitable work, polar explorer Rebecca Lee Lok-sze became an important influence. She introduced him to Richard Bach’s Jonathan Livingston Seagull, the story of a bird unwilling to accept the limits imposed by its flock.
Cheung said a person’s starting point should not determine how far they could go. In his view, school results capture only one point in someone’s life; what follows depends on the choices and actions that come afterwards.
His studies eventually took him to Canada, where he completed a PhD in glaciology at Queen’s University. His doctoral research examined decades of glacier change in Auyuittuq and Sirmilik national parks in the Canadian Arctic.
Cheung said he did not gauge success by how much he earned. He cared more about the knowledge and experience gained, and whether his work could contribute something useful.
He now gives young people opportunities to experience field science themselves. On the Swiss trip, students were asked to observe each glacier closely and explain how it differed from the previous one.
By the end of the programme, the students had a grasp of what the ice and surrounding terrain could tell them, he said.

Some participants in his youth programmes have since pursued their own paths. One later studied in Tasmania and went on to work in Antarctica. Another headed to France to train as a mountain guide.
Cheung also recalled a girl who had repeated a year at school and was considering giving up on an examination she feared. He promised that if she passed, he would send her a postcard from the Arctic. She did, and he kept his promise.
Donors including Christine Yu and Cyrus Cuthbertson have helped fund his youth programme, while PlayHard Hong Kong has supplied some of the field equipment. Cheung hopes that support could reach pupils who might otherwise be unable to take part.
Years of polar fieldwork have also taught him that even careful plans can unravel.
On his first assignment in the Canadian Arctic in 2022, a helicopter due to collect him was involved in an accident before reaching him. Cheung waited for 10 days before he could leave. The pilot was seriously injured and had to be taken to hospital.
“Being able to come home, see my mother and talk to her, that’s success,” he said.
The lesson from the polar regions, he said, is to prepare carefully while accepting that conditions can change without warning.
“We make a plan so that we have a plan to change,” he said. “Every day you wake up to a different problem, and you have to find a way to solve it.”

data.title: Worker prospects in hair, beauty sector not cut and dried amid staff shortages
data.description:
Hongkonger Terrence Wu Chung-ting puts on an apron, picks up a comb and massages hair essence into a client’s scalp during a treatment for hair loss.
But eight years ago, Wu’s job could not have been any more different. A finance graduate from one of the city’s top universities, he was then a marketer for beauty products and focused on sales.
But when he saw untapped potential in Hong Kong’s hairdressing industry, he boldly switched careers from a white-collar to a blue-collar profession, training to become a scalp therapist.
Wu, now in his mid-thirties, recalled starting from scratch by learning basic tasks such as shampooing and blow-drying hair.
Beauty care and hairdressing were recently highlighted in the government’s midterm manpower projection report as a job category expected to see a manpower crunch.
The report said the city’s workforce was expected to shrink by about 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages forecast across industries involving both skilled technical workers and low-skilled labourers.
There were 49,800 workers in the beauty care and hairdressing industry in 2025, with a 4.9 per cent vacancy rate, according to statistics from the Labour and Welfare Bureau.
The industry would need 2,440 more workers, with hairdressers specifically in demand.
An industry expert said salons struggled to fill junior vacancies because roles with low entry requirements attracted mostly young people who constantly changed jobs, resulting in high turnover.

Noting the staffing problems in the industry, Wu said salon assistants might not be aware of the career prospects in the hair care sector.
“I think most people do not really know much about hair and scalp treatment, and that could be the cause of the manpower shortage in this industry,” he said.
“They don’t even know about the position of a scalp therapist, so they don’t consider this a viable career path,” Wu said.
Unlike traditional salons where assistants must do the grunt work of cleaning the salon before learning haircutting techniques and other skills, the training of a scalp therapist focuses on developing knowledge, including a basic understanding of scalp health.
In Wu’s salon, a single hair and scalp treatment session can range from HK$1,000 (US$127) to more than HK$2,000 depending on the client’s needs.
When he first started, Wu studied the stylists from traditional hair salons, learning how to blow-dry and style women’s hair and other skills.
“I guess that to outsiders, it might seem unexpected – they probably wonder why someone highly educated would choose to go into blue-collar work,” he said.
“But I see this as an industry where you can actually make good money. Even though it’s hard work, the returns are worth it.”

Nelson Ip Sai-hung, founding chairman of the Federation of Beauty Industry, acknowledged that young salon assistants often came and went because they knew the shops were always hiring for junior roles.
But scalp treatment was a step up and represented a “high-value-added” item in the industry, he said.
“I think it is pretty attractive to youngsters … honestly, [the treatment] is a high-value transaction, which means the revenue will be high too,” Ip said.
In addition, the title of “therapist” made a good impression and conferred a certain status that was “not just an ordinary apprentice”, he added.

Elaine Wan Yee-man, director of United Beauty Group, said it was difficult to hire beauticians for massage and facial services, as the work was physically demanding and many preferred to be therapists who operated equipment instead.
“The biggest problem we face in recruitment is that candidates divide themselves into therapists and beauticians. They feel being a beautician is quite an ordinary role, but there should not be such a prejudice,” she said.
“I think a proper facial should include massage – pressing the face, shoulders and neck – that is what makes it a full treatment.”
Wan said the industry was struggling to attract new blood because apprentice salaries ranged from HK$10,000 to HK$18,000 a month. The “bundled arrangements” that once guaranteed workers a basic pay regardless of their output had also been scrapped, creating a sense of income instability for new hires.
“When the market was good, everyone was poaching staff. It was really important to have bundled arrangements, and workers could push their salaries up really high,” she said.
“But now the market is genuinely worse, so a lot of us in the beauty industry have already cancelled the bundled arrangement.”
She added that there was still demand for beauticians who provided facial treatments manually, as many customers were willing to pay for these traditional treatments.

data.title: Singaporean teenager flown to hospital after falling ill during Lion Rock hike
data.description:
A Singaporean girl has been flown to a hospital after falling ill during a hike with two other friends at Hong Kong’s Lion Rock, according to police.
The force received a report on Saturday from the mother of one of the hikers at about 6.50am.
Her daughter called for help after the 17-year-old Singaporean friend vomited and experienced chills during their hike at Lion Rock, a 495-metre-high mountain.
Police later arrived at the scene while the Government Flying Service deployed a helicopter to airlift the teenager. The girl, who remained conscious, was sent to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai for treatment.
The other two girls, both 17, sustained no injuries and returned home.

data.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: Blind musician with birth disease plays her heart out
data.description:
A year after a seven-hour surgery in Hong Kong in 2025, Cassie Li Pui-ying was on stage at Queen Elizabeth Stadium, playing the drums before an audience of more than 2,500 people. She heard the applause but could not see who it came from.
That March night was organised by Live Theatre, which her mother Marine Mak also helps run. Li sang, spoke and played the drums. The group gives visually impaired students a stage to perform on.
Despite having been through several serious health scares, what comes across is Li’s faith, optimism and cheer. She moves people.
For the second year in a row, the 17-year-old has been named a finalist in the perseverance category of the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
Launched in 2013, the awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed.
Recounting her tribulations in the past year – only the latest in a lifetime of health challenges – Li said she struggled to accept her situation when she was readmitted to the intensive care unit of Queen Mary Hospital in 2025.
“I wanted a normal life. Why another operation?” she said.
But her surgeon, who has looked after Li since childhood, was reassuring. “If you believe us, we’ll help you. And you’ll be all right,” she recalled him saying.

Born with Hirschsprung’s disease, Li lacks the nerve cells that push food through the gut.
Doctors once expected her to live only about 10 months. She cannot eat as others do, and is fed intravenously each day. She is blind in her left eye and has only 10 per cent of sight remaining in her right.
Li spent years of her childhood going in and out of hospital. She often had little appetite. But music captivated her from a young age and, despite her disability, she learned how to play different instruments.
She is currently in Form Four on an adapted curriculum and hopes to take applied learning in music. Apart from drumming, she is learning to play the guitar and to write music on a keyboard.
Enlarged sheet music helps, while tactile markers on the guitar frets and a tuning app make playing easier. She learns how to play songs note by note, and by ear, and enjoys performing while leaving the mixing to others.
Li said she hopes eventually to pursue a career in music, whether through performing, songwriting or other work in the industry.

Li has drawn on her years of struggle, not only with her health problems but also in other personal experiences, to build resilience and to help others.
Her father passed away six years ago, when she was just 11, but what she carries today is not a sense of loss but the fondest memories of him.
“This moment was very sweet,” she said, describing a photograph of him holding her as a young child.
Li said she was grateful for all the people who had supported her over the years, including her mother, her teachers and all the doctors and nurses in the paediatric ward at Queen Mary Hospital.
Their encouragement and care, she said, had helped her through difficult times and continued to motivate her to keep learning, performing and looking ahead.

data.title: Lack of heat plan leaves Hong Kong’s vulnerable residents at risk, experts warn
data.description:
Environmentalists and academics have criticised the omission of a systemic heat-health action plan in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and latest policy address, warning that relying on “common sense” is failing to protect vulnerable residents from rising temperatures.
Their comments came as new research from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) found that extreme heat may have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in the city over the past decade.
In response to the South China Morning Post’s queries about the lack of a cross-departmental heat action plan for vulnerable groups, a government spokesman said there were ongoing efforts to “elevate the response capabilities of the government and the community”.
Environmentalists noted that neither the five-year blueprint nor the annual policy address, both delivered by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in September, included a comprehensive plan for a systemic, overarching heat-health action plan to address urban heat. A new management system known as the “city brain”, which aims to improve interdepartmental collaboration during extreme weather, was proposed in the policy address.


The World Health Organization outlines eight core elements for heat-health action plans, including governance, early-warning systems, surveillance and outreach.
Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner Prudence Yeung said: “Through high-level political commitment, such as including a heat action plan in the policy address or the five-year plan, [the government] could ensure heat adaptation and resilience as a citywide priority, and provide a foundation for investment in heat resilience infrastructure, research and public awareness.”
A Greenpeace survey, released in August, found that nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported physical or mental distress during periods of extreme heat. That month the city logged its hottest single day – August 9 – since records began in 1884.
In a study currently under peer review, Professor David Bishai, director of the school of public health at HKU, and other researchers revised figures from research in 2024, estimating that heatwaves in Hong Kong between 2014 and 2023 may have contributed between 1,455 and 3,238 excess deaths. The earlier estimate was 1,677 excess deaths.

Bishai’s projection was based on demographic data from the Census and Statistics Department, temperature data from the Hong Kong Observatory and relative risks derived from local research. A simulation was used to estimate heat-attributable deaths under different definitions of a heatwave.
These preventable excess deaths had largely gone unrecognised as they were preventable exacerbations of underlying illnesses, rather than heatstroke, which was rare, Bishai said.
“Enacting an action plan in the face of extreme heat can be helpful in reducing death rates … We know that just leaving it to common sense is not working, because we are still seeing these excess deaths during heatwaves,” he said.
“It’s like running a marathon. The heart rate goes up, the blood vessels dilate, blood is shunted away from the brain into the hands and feet so that you can sweat more. And it is a very bad stress test that people’s bodies fail at those ages with those pre-existing conditions.”
Bishai cited Paris, where a heat action plan featuring proactive welfare checks on the elderly was projected to have cut heat-related mortality by around 77 per cent following heatwaves in 2003.
Hong Kong’s heat measures are activated when the Observatory issues a “very hot weather” warning, triggering the opening of temporary shelters in community halls. According to government figures, the 19 shelters that operated overnight on very hot evenings served between 120 and 210 users a day in June and July.
The Labour Department issues heat-stress alerts for outdoor workers – recently revamped following criticism – while the Department of Health provides public health advisories.




Ren Chao, an HKU professor who specialises in climate-responsive design, pointed to a gap between heat warnings and government-led community relief. She called for government intervention through more heat shelters and public health education, as well as ventilation and electricity bill subsidies.
Heat-risk mapping was also crucial to visualise areas experiencing hot days and nights, which varied across districts, and served as a powerful tool for communicating heat risks to the public, she said.
Ren said the government could consider adopting a coordination framework similar to that of its existing typhoon response panel to develop a heat action plan.
The Home Affairs Department said in a reply to the SCMP that care teams would remind households in need of measures to stay cool during hot weather, but it did not provide information on the number of visits carried out on hot days.
A Development Bureau spokeswoman said the government was committed to enhancing urban forestry resilience and integrating greening into public works and new developments, to “build a more sustainable, climate-resilient and liveable Hong Kong”.
The Observatory had been closely providing meteorological data and meteorological advice to help government departments formulate appropriate responses to heat, a spokeswoman said.

data.title: Hong Kong lawmakers back 5-year plan as firms urged to align with blueprint
data.description:
Hong Kong’s legislature has passed motions supporting the city’s first five-year plan and thanking Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu for his latest policy address, while Beijing’s top representative in the city urged mainland Chinese enterprises to align themselves with the government’s blueprint.
At the close of a three-day Legislative Council debate on Friday, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki thanked lawmakers for their suggestions, saying they would help improve governance.
“The process of formulating the city’s five-year plan and the in-depth discussion at the Legislative Council have demonstrated a positive interaction between the administration and the legislature, with both striving for the best for Hong Kong,” he said.
“I believe that, as long as we work together, remain proactive and pragmatic, we will be able to fully implement the five-year plan, create a better future for residents and make Hong Kong a bridge connecting China and the world.”
While backing the two motions, lawmaker Junius Ho Kwan-yiu said the five-year plan had plenty of content but lacked concrete targets.

Ho pointed to the document’s description of annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth as remaining “within a reasonable range” and Lee’s explanation that Hong Kong’s economy was subject to external factors.
“I hope the government can show more determination,” Ho said.
Lee unveiled the annual policy address last month alongside the five-year plan, which aims to align Hong Kong’s development with the national development strategy.
The two documents set out initiatives to accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject and strengthen the city’s position in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.
Some lawmakers highlighted the government’s coming tasks, such as rebuilding public confidence in the malpractice-plagued building maintenance market following the deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court in November last year that killed 168 people and displaced about 5,000.
Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan urged the government to consider setting up a statutory body to supervise building maintenance works and introducing third-party construction cost assessments, among other measures, to stamp out back-room deals and bid-rigging.
Fellow lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu backed a suggestion to establish a dedicated authority to monitor building renovations, saying that overcoming gridlock was an “inevitable reform”.

Separately, Zhou Ji, director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong, urged mainland enterprises operating in the city to align themselves with the government’s first five-year plan and play a greater role in its economic development.
Speaking at a reception hosted by a business group on Friday, Zhou outlined three expectations for mainland firms, including that they capitalise on Hong Kong’s advantages under the “one country, two systems” principle to cultivate new growth drivers.
He also called on companies to leverage Hong Kong’s position as a gateway to international markets, work closely with the government’s task force supporting mainland businesses expanding overseas, and attract more enterprises to establish a presence in the city.
Zhou further urged firms to strengthen their grass-roots engagement and charitable work to improve residents’ livelihoods and sense of well-being.

data.title: Anthropic claims Chinese AI firms secretly use Claude. Is it true?
data.description:
Did Chinese AI companies secretly tap US models to close the technology gap? That is the central question hanging over China’s tech sector following a wave of allegations from Washington and American AI lab Anthropic.
According to a joint advisory by the National Security Agency, FBI, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency last month, Chinese AI developers have been systematically extracting capabilities from US frontier models to reduce their own computing, electricity and research costs.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent similarly warned in July that Chinese firms were engaged in large-scale “distillation”.
Specifically, Anthropic claimed Chinese AI developers used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to siphon reasoning data from its flagship model, Claude – and in some cases even used the US model as a covert back end for their own apps.
Here’s a closer look at whether the accusations hold water – and why Beijing is taking those claims seriously.
What are Anthropic’s allegations?
Anthropic accused Chinese developers of conducting “industrial-scale” distillation, a technique in which outputs from a more capable “teacher” model are used to improve another model.
While model distillation is a common practice across the AI industry, Anthropic claimed Chinese firms crossed ethical lines. According to a report published by the company last month, Chinese labs circumvented usage restrictions through fraudulent accounts and third-party proxy services to harvest Claude’s output and reasoning traces at scale.
Anthropic reported that over just 10 days, Moonshot routed almost 300,000 user requests, primarily to the Opus model. The Chinese company utilised a proxy network of 5,380 fraudulent accounts largely based in Singapore and Japan, Anthropic claimed.
Furthermore, Anthropic alleged that some companies used Claude as a hidden back end. This meant users believed they were interacting with a domestic Chinese model when their queries were actually being processed by the US firm’s servers, the firm said.
Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment.

How strong is the evidence?
Industry analysts are divided over the credibility and attribution of Anthropic’s findings.
Konstantin Pilz, co-founder and fellow at the Washington-based Centre for Technology and Statecraft, considered the claims credible, noting that they reflected the intense pressure on Chinese developers facing US chip export restrictions.
“To not fall further behind on AI model performance, Chinese AI companies have to use adversarial distillation on a large scale,” Pilz said, suggesting that distillation allowed domestic developers to leapfrog expensive reasoning data generation.
Ben Hayum, a research assistant at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said Anthropic had long been able to gather threat-intelligence signals that could detect and attribute distillation attacks.
However, other experts argued that pinpointing direct blame on Chinese AI companies was not always straightforward.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, noted that third-party proxy services – or “transfer stations” – might be the real culprits. These proxies might secretly divert user requests to Claude to obtain and sell reasoning data without the direct involvement of the Chinese AI labs, he said.
Wang Zebin, an investment manager at Shenzhen-based private equity firm JG Investment focused on large language models and embodied intelligence, said Anthropic’s report “does not provide enough concrete examples to independently verify how those companies obtained or used the model outputs”, adding that the specific distillation methods described in the report were questionable.
Why might Beijing be concerned?
Chinese regulators were reportedly investigating domestic AI labs following Anthropic’s report. According to a report by The Information last month, the Cyberspace Administration of China questioned seven developers named by Anthropic before narrowing its focus to DeepSeek and Moonshot.
DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.
If the report was true, the main concern for Beijing would not be intellectual property theft or model copying, but data security, according to Pilz.
Anthropic claimed that some of the prompts sent to Claude contained sensitive information from state-affiliated organisations and companies, as well as names, email addresses, and other corporate data.
Re-routing sensitive data to American AI model providers may pose a “very significant security issue for China”, Chan said, adding that it would be “even more severe” than exposing search histories because users share so much data with AI. Coding requests in particular can leak underlying IT infrastructure or login credentials.
“China should be seriously questioning this,” Hayum said, noting that regulators must evaluate whether they can trust domestic tech firms to safeguard sensitive data and manage emerging cybersecurity risks.
Even if the allegations were true, however, Chan expected Beijing to handle the matter discreetly to avoid publicly validating Anthropic’s claims.
Additional reporting by Minxiao Chang

data.title: As Hong Kong pushes liquidity reforms, will they be enough to draw capital?
data.description:
Hong Kong’s securities watchdog is renewing its push to boost market liquidity, setting out further reforms as emerging markets grapple with capital outflow pressure amid a rally in US equities and a strengthening dollar.
Speaking at a conference organised by the Asian Securities & Financial Markets Association (Asifma) on Friday, Julia Leung, CEO of the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), outlined measures ranging from extended trading hours and shorter settlement cycles to cross-market margining and board lot reform aimed at improving market liquidity and efficiency.
“The SFC is working with the HKEX [Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing] to develop margin offsets across its clearing houses,” Leung said, adding that the move would free up capital for “more productive” uses.
Leung also said the HKEX’s clearing house, OTC Clear, would enable same-day settlement for bond deposits and withdrawals later this year, streamlining the process and making non-cash collateral “a more attractive funding pool”.
As part of board lot reform, Leung announced the introduction of eight standardised categories. The maximum board lot value would be capped at HK$50,000 (US$6,370), while the minimum would be reduced to HK$1,000.
“The aim is to lower entry barriers, broaden participation and make stock trading more accessible,” she said.
The measure will take effect in November for existing issuers, having already been implemented for new listings since July.
Average daily turnover in Hong Kong’s stock market had exceeded HK$270 billion so far this year, up 160 per cent from 2023, SFC data showed. The increase had been driven partly by mainland Chinese funds flowing into Hong Kong through the Stock Connect and Bond Connect programmes, particularly into technology shares.
Hong Kong had also become Asia’s third-largest exchange-traded product (ETP) market by turnover, according to the SFC.
Challenges remain, however, as global investors continue to favour US assets. Nasdaq and the S&P 500 hit record highs this week amid enthusiasm for artificial intelligence-related investments, while the Hang Seng Index has fallen about 5.5 per cent this year.
Leung also said the HKEX would soon announce a timeline for shortening the market’s settlement cycle to T+1 – allowing trades to be settled one business day after execution – from T+2.
“Shortening the cycle reduces various risks, improves capital efficiency and brings Hong Kong more in line with major international markets,” she said.
The US adopted T+1 settlement in 2024, while the European Union, UK and Switzerland plan to make the transition in October 2027.
Peter Stein, CEO of Asifma, said the association supported the move towards T+1, but had “expressed concerns about the implementation timeline” during the consultation process.
Given Hong Kong’s time difference with New York, “you have a narrower window with which to provide the funding to settle trades and do the [foreign exchange] conversions”, he said.
Stein added that he welcomed the new measures announced by Leung and viewed them as “a great model for what we’d like to see happen in some other markets”.

data.title: Developer of One Stanley pledges 6-year warranty and checks amid steel bar probe
data.description:
The developer of One Stanley has offered flat owners a six-year structural warranty and free independent property inspections amid an investigation into suspected steel reinforcement deficiencies at the seaside luxury residential development in southern Hong Kong.
K Wise, a subsidiary of One Stanley developer K&K Property, addressed the brewing scandal on Friday, a week after allegations of substandard work were reported by a local property media outlet, issuing a statement outlining remedial measures for homeowners and buyers completing transactions.
“The company understands that the incident has caused concern among property owners, buyers and the public, and will make building safety and safeguarding the interests of owners its top priority,” K Wise said.
“On top of the three-year defect liability period already provided by our company, we will also offer a six-year structural warranty from the date of completion of the purchase.”
It added: “[We will] ... also arrange independent, qualified professionals to conduct property inspections for owners and buyers, and all costs will be covered”.
The online property news platform claimed that an on-site inspection of a house found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts of the home.
The number fell short by as much as 75 per cent from the approved building plans, according to the report.
The property in question is a four-bedroom, 3,000 square foot (278 square metre) detached house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024 for about HK$100 million (US$12.7 million).
The irregularities were subsequently spotted by engineers and contractors hired by the owner during internal renovations, according to the report.
The owner made a report to the Buildings Department, which revealed last week it had been carrying out inspections at the development since March.
The department has also asked the developer to submit a report.
In Friday’s statement, K Wise said it had contacted the owner of the detached house in question to discuss follow-up plans.
It said it had proposed that “both parties jointly hire an independent professional to conduct further inspections to clarify the circumstances”.
But no consensus was reached, according to K Wise.
Both sides had also discussed related claims but no agreement was reached either, the company said.
“Regarding the private contracts and legal matters between the two parties, our company is not prepared to make further comments,” K Wise said.
On follow-up actions, the company said it had contacted owners who had completed their transactions and was continuing to reach out to buyers who were currently in the process of making a transaction.
“As the investigation is ongoing, it is not appropriate for our company to comment on unverified technical matters at this stage so as to avoid making speculations or biased judgments before the completion of the investigation,” it said.
The South China Morning Post has learned that 24 transactions were recorded at One Stanley between March and September.

data.title: Travel agencies tout Huanggang Port tours, but security chief urges later visits
data.description:
Some Hong Kong travel agencies are offering tours featuring “five-minute clearance” at the revamped Huanggang Port when it opens on Monday, but the security chief has urged those who do not need to use the crossing immediately to delay their visits.
Three days before the port’s official opening, the South China Morning Post on Friday found a number of tour packages advertised on social media that promoted the redeveloped border checkpoint as a new attraction on trips to mainland China.
An advertisement posted by Sino Step Travel Services on its Facebook page said: “Early access to the Huanggang Port for a brand new clearance experience!”
Marketing manager Cici Chung Ka-lam said: “Since the government announced early Friday that the checkpoint would open at 6.30am on October 12, inquiries and bookings have risen markedly, with many residents eager to experience ‘five-minute clearance’.”
She added that the checkpoint complex had “become a key selling point” of the agency’s tours.

Big Line Holiday began preparing tours through the new checkpoint in early September and started selling short-haul trips to Guangdong priced at about HK$1,000 to HK$2,000.
Sales director Kit Chan said the first tour sold out within two to three hours of going on sale. The agency now has 10 groups departing next Monday, each with about 40 people, most of them older travellers.
“We have trained all our call centre and frontline staff to stress the new Huanggang checkpoint as the biggest selling point, which has the ‘joint inspection’ system to make clearance much faster and more efficient,” he said.
“The two-border, two-check arrangement at the old Huanggang checkpoint was always a bit troublesome,” Chan said, adding that “many tour members told us that having to pull their luggage and transfer from buses was very inconvenient.”
Chan said the company would arrange more tours through Huanggang if the checkpoint operated smoothly and passenger numbers remained manageable.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that authorities had allocated extra manpower and drawn up contingency plans to cope with unexpected surges in passenger numbers, anticipating strong interest in the revamped border crossing.
“We understand that during the initial opening, some tour groups may view Huanggang Port as a new attraction, lingering a little longer during border clearance to take extra photos, which we consider completely understandable,” he said.
“We have fully anticipated this situation. At the same time, we appeal to members of the public who are in no real rush to consider experiencing the facility at a later date.”
Tang also warned that travellers should proceed with border clearance as soon as possible after entering the building, as failing to do so could constitute a breach of the law.

data.title: US lawmakers push green card bill for Hongkongers, but observers doubt success
data.description:
Two US lawmakers are pushing for a bill that would allow Hongkongers in the country to apply for permanent residency, but authorities and observers have dismissed it as a political move unlikely to succeed.
Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, and Representative James McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, announced the Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act, seeking to provide a pathway to green cards and ultimately citizenship for Hong Kong residents in the US currently protected under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme.
Introducing the bill, Merkley accused Beijing and Hong Kong authorities of continuing to “undermine the fundamental rights and freedoms of Hongkongers”.
“The United States must protect Hong Kong residents who have sought refuge in America,” he said. “Congress must take action and enact our legislation to ensure Hongkongers residing in the US do not have to fear deportation.”
The proposal drew criticism from both the Hong Kong and central governments.
A Hong Kong government spokesman denounced the remarks as “unfounded and biased”, saying that authorities “steadfastly safeguarded the rights and freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong people as protected under the law.”
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement to the South China Morning Post that Hong Kong affairs were purely China’s internal matters, in which no foreign government, force, organisation or individual could interfere.
“China urges some members of the US Congress to stop pushing for the review of relevant bills concerning Hong Kong and to stop meddling in Hong Kong affairs and interfering in China’s internal affairs,” it said.

Wilson Chan Wai-shun, co-founder of the Pagoda Institute think tank, said on Friday that the bill was very likely to perish in the current legislative session, and there would be insufficient time to process the proposal in the next session before DED protection expired on February 5, 2027.
He explained that US lawmakers would focus on campaigns surrounding the midterm election in November, while the new batch of lawmakers, to be sworn in in early January, could not process the bill quickly because they would have to handle procedural matters.
“If it cannot be realised within the current legislative session, there will not be enough time in the next session to cover the date when DED expires,” he said. “Then effectively, it would become useless.”
DED is an executive measure that temporarily protects Hongkongers from deportation and allows them to work, but does not offer permanent legal status.
It was introduced in 2021 by the Biden administration in response to Beijing’s imposition of the national security law on Hong Kong and was extended twice in 2023 and 2025 by the then president. It is not yet clear whether US President Donald Trump will renew it.
Under the proposed bill, Hong Kong permanent residents and their families staying in the US relying on the programme would be able to apply for permanent residency, provided that they had been staying in the country continuously since January 15, 2025, without having returned to Hong Kong or mainland China.

The proposal comes amid the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown, including moves to end Temporary Protected Status – which shields migrants from deportation and allows them to work – for people from more than a dozen countries, including Venezuela, Haiti and Honduras.
Chan said although the Republicans’ and Democrats’ stances on China remained highly consistent, the bill also involved migration issues and might leave the Republican Party, which controls both chambers of Congress, with reservations.
“[Republicans] do not have to explicitly object to the bill, but could just insist that it be deliberated through normal procedures,” he said. “In that case, the bill is already dragged to death.”
Keeping full control over DED gives Trump significant leverage both as a diplomatic bargaining chip with Beijing and on domestic immigration, according to Chan.
McGovern’s office told the SCMP that the issue had drawn Republican support before, citing the bipartisan Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act that Marco Rubio, then a senator and now secretary of state, introduced in 2021.
Congress had tried multiple times to help Hongkongers settle in the US, without success.
Two bills introduced in 2020 – the Hong Kong Victims of Communism Support Act and the Hong Kong Refugee Protection Act – would have offered Hong Kong residents asylum or priority refugee status.
In the same year, the House passed the Hong Kong People’s Freedom and Choice Act, which would have given Hongkongers temporary protected status.
However, Republican Senator Ted Cruz blocked it in the Senate, arguing it could let Chinese spies into the US.

data.title: Soaring component costs force laptop makers to rethink shift away from China
data.description:
Notebook manufacturers are being forced to rethink their shift out of China and consider moving production back to the manufacturing hub, as skyrocketing component costs squeeze profit margins, according to market research firm TrendForce.
The Taiwan-based firm projected that the share of global notebook production outside mainland China would decline to 21 per cent this year from about 24 per cent in 2025, and drop below 20 per cent in 2027.
“This suggests that brands are reassessing the balance between supply-chain diversification and manufacturing efficiency as policy and cost conditions evolve,” TrendForce said in a report released on Thursday.
Over the past few years, major laptop vendors have expanded their manufacturing footprints outside China to hedge against trade tariffs and geopolitical friction.
US computer giant Dell, for example, set a goal in 2023 to phase out Chinese-made chips by 2024 and move about half its production out of China by 2025, while Apple shifted portions of its device assembly to Vietnam and India.

However, unless trade barriers escalate significantly, financial pragmatism was reasserting itself over risk mitigation, according to TrendForce.
“If tariff pressures do not intensify further, the factors guiding manufacturing ‘glocalisation’ are likely to shift from minimising policy risks towards production costs, supply-chain completeness and operational efficiency,” the firm said.
The predicted strategic pivot comes as the personal computer (PC) industry braces for subdued consumer demand driven by rising component prices. TrendForce estimated that global notebook shipments would fall by a low single digits percentage in 2027.
If semiconductor costs kept climbing, however, laptop brands would have little choice but to pass more of those expenses on to buyers, potentially deepening the market contraction to a high single digits decline, the firm said.
Core hardware has grown increasingly expensive. TrendForce estimated that central processing units (CPUs), dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and solid-state drives (SSDs) collectively accounted for around 68 per cent of the total bill of materials for a mainstream US$900 laptop in the third quarter.
Compounding the pressure, global PC shipments plunged about 20 per cent year on year to 62.7 million units in the third quarter, according to a separate report by research firm IDC on Thursday.
Jitesh Ubrani, research director for consumer devices at IDC, attributed the drop to stockpiling by vendors in the first half of the year as they sought to get ahead of memory price hikes. This created an “inventory pull-in earlier in the year”, leaving the third quarter with “little demand to draw on”, IDC said.
“Prices will remain elevated,” Ubrani said. “With macro conditions worsening, the risk is that the outlook for the next few quarters gets worse before it gets better.”
Industry market shares remained largely intact despite the downturn.
China’s Lenovo retained its top spot with a 23.8 per cent global share, despite a 22.6 per cent drop in shipments in the third quarter, IDC data showed. HP held second place with a 16.5 per cent share, hit by a 30.9 per cent decline in shipments. Dell ranked third, with shipments falling 25 per cent during the quarter.

data.title: Girl filmed carrying beer bags to be placed in temporary care with siblings
data.description:
A 10-year-old Hong Kong girl filmed carrying heavy bags of beer will be placed in temporary care with her two siblings after welfare assessments found it would “not be suitable” for them to return home following the arrest of their parents on suspicion of ill-treating a child.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that the three children were still in hospital for health checks and were expected to be discharged later that day or on Saturday.
“Even after the three siblings are discharged from hospital, the Social Welfare Department’s assessment is that it will not be suitable for them to return home immediately,” he said.
“We have therefore arranged suitable temporary accommodation for them after their discharge.”
Sun added that the siblings might not be able to stay together because of their age differences.
He also said authorities would hold a multidisciplinary case conference on child abuse as soon as possible, with social workers, teachers, medical personnel and police taking part.
The conference would review the children’s family circumstances, care needs, safety risks and long-term welfare requirements before a plan was drawn up, he said.
“The next step depends on the final assessment and recommendations of the multidisciplinary case conference,” Sun said.
“If appropriate, one possible direction would be to apply to the court for a care or protection order.”

Police arrested the girl’s mother, 32, and stepfather, 38, on Wednesday on suspicion of ill-treatment of a child after the girl was filmed carrying two heavy bags of beer at Fu Tai Estate in Tuen Mun, with her backpack torn and gaping open.
The video showed the man, who was with two other children, snatching one of the bags back and calling the girl “useless” when bystanders intervened.
The pair were released on bail on Thursday and must report back to police later this month.
The girl’s school, Lutheran Tsang Shing Siu Leun School, said on Wednesday that social workers and teachers had provided counselling to the pupil and her family.
The Education Bureau said it was “highly concerned” and confirmed that the school had activated its crisis management team.
In Hong Kong, the maximum penalty for ill-treatment or neglect of a child or young person is 10 years’ imprisonment upon conviction on indictment, or three years’ imprisonment upon summary conviction.

data.title: News commentator denies unlawfully revealing police meeting details online
data.description:
A Hong Kong news commentator accused of violating the national security law has denied exposing police intelligence operations, telling a court that details of his meeting with officers were already public knowledge before he posted them online.
Wong Kwok-ngon, 72, who ran a YouTube commentary channel under the pen name Wong On-yin, stood trial at the District Court on Friday. He is the first person in Hong Kong to be prosecuted for allegedly prejudicing an investigation into national security offences by unlawfully disclosing details of a police interview.
He was also charged with knowingly publishing seditious publications in connection with videos covering local and international news.
In court, Wong questioned why two sergeants from the police force’s National Security Department considered their meeting with him on December 2, 2025, confidential when media outlets had already widely reported that he was under investigation.
Wong and other residents had planned to hold a press conference that day about the Wang Fuk Court blaze, which killed 168 people last November. But the event was called off after national security officers invited them to a meeting the same day.
Wong posted two videos on his YouTube channel the following day discussing the meeting.
Prosecutors said in their opening submission that Wong’s commentary had exceeded the bounds of “fair comment” because he repeatedly portrayed the National Security Department’s operations as a tool of suppression.
They said Wong had signed a non-disclosure declaration at the start of the December 2 meeting, agreeing to keep everything discussed confidential.
The court heard that Wong, a highly educated former employee of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, told Sergeants Li Pak-him and Wong Ping-kiu that he understood the terms.

Li said Wong did not ask any questions about the declaration but asked whether he was under investigation.
Sergeant Wong said the purpose of the meeting was to gather intelligence from the commentator, who was not a suspect at the time, and assess whether the planned press conference might pose a national security risk.
Both officers testified that they had asked him about the background to the press conference.
Li said he had reiterated the confidentiality requirement at the end of the hour-long meeting.
Wong asked Li: “I replied to you at the time that it was already in the newspaper that you guys were having a meeting with me, so what exactly do you want me to keep confidential?”
The commentator said he had told the officers he intended only to explain legal matters at the press conference and would not disclose any sensitive information that should concern them.
Li said he had reiterated that the “entire meeting”, including the fact that it had taken place, should be kept private.
He added that he had not expected to have to tell Wong what he could and could not say to his viewers.
The trial will continue on Monday, when the court will hear evidence about the allegedly seditious content published on Wong’s channel.

data.title: DFI Retail Group says it will continue to invest in Hong Kong supermarkets
data.description:
Hong Kong-headquartered DFI Retail Group, which owns and operates the city’s largest supermarket network, says it will continue to invest in new stores even though consumers remain cautious.
Darren Chan, the group’s managing director for food in Hong Kong and Macau, said DFI – whose supermarket chains include Wellcome and Market Place in Hong Kong – was also “looking for opportunities to strengthen” its network where there was “clear customer demand and attractive long-term returns”.
“We invest in both new stores and our existing stores,” Chan said. “We open stores where they can better serve local communities, while continuing to modernise our existing network to ensure our store remains attractive, convenient and relevant to evolving customer needs.”
Wellcome, Market Place, 3hreesixty and Oliver’s operate a network of more than 325 stores serving more than 14 million customers a month.
Chan also oversees 3hreesixty, Oliver’s and San Miu, a supermarket chain in Macau.
In the first half of the year, DFI’s food division posted 1.4 per cent growth in sales to US$1.14 billion, although same-store sales declined by 0.2 per cent.
The group has been employing new strategies to improve sales as more Hong Kong residents travel to Shenzhen for cheaper shopping and dining options. They include broadening the number of countries it imports from to help bring prices down.
There is no one-size-fits-all approach
Darren Chan, DFI
Wellcome and Market Place have recently teamed up with CJ Foods, South Korea’s largest food company, to enhance their Korean food offerings, with DFI saying the collaboration is expected to generate more than US$22 million in sales.
Meanwhile, Market Place recently launched “Taste of Australia”, a gourmet food fair featuring more than 70 Australian brands and over 200 new products including fresh produce, wines and snacks.
Chan said Wellcome’s real estate strategy would continue to feature large and small stores.
“There is no one-size-fits-all approach,” he said. “The optimal format depends on factors such as catchment demographics, customer shopping missions and local market opportunities.”
Hong Kong’s overall retail sales rose by 8.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of this year, but stand-alone supermarket sales rose by just 1.4 per cent according to the Census and Statistics Department. Sales of all supermarkets, including those in department stores, rose by 1.5 per cent.
Formerly known as Dairy Farm, DFI also owns and operates Mannings, 7-Eleven and Ikea in Hong Kong. It also operates Guardian in Southeast Asia, 7-Eleven in Macau, Guangdong province and Singapore and Ikea in Macau, Taiwan and Indonesia.

data.title: China state funds double down on Hua Hong in legacy chip push
data.description:
Chinese state funds are ramping up support for the country’s second-largest contract chipmaker, pouring billions of yuan into the parent of Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor and a new manufacturing facility to fuel Beijing’s drive for self-reliance in mature-node chips.
The capital blitz, spanning Hua Hong’s Shanghai-based parent company and a fabrication plant in Wuxi, highlights how government-coordinated financing is doubling down on domestic foundries, as Washington tightens technology restrictions on China.
Registered capital of Hua Hong Group, the Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed chipmaker’s owner, surged to 19.7 billion yuan (US$2.9 billion) from 13.5 billion yuan, according to a stock exchange filing on Thursday. The 6.2 billion yuan injection was led by Shanghai Guosheng Group, a state-backed investment vehicle.
Following the transaction, Guosheng’s direct stake in Hua Hong Group would jump to 41.7 per cent from 15.3 per cent, while its indirect holding would rise to 10.2 per cent from 3.8 per cent.
The Shanghai State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission – the local state-assets regulator – also injected 19.7 million yuan, maintaining its role as Hua Hong Group’s ultimate actual controller.
Blocked by the US from acquiring the most advanced chipmaking equipment, including extreme ultraviolet lithography systems, Beijing has channelled state funds towards dominating legacy and mature-node semiconductors, generally defined as chips made using 28-nanometre process technology and above.
While less sophisticated than cutting-edge artificial intelligence processors, legacy chips remain essential for electric vehicles, industrial automation, Internet of Things devices and consumer electronics.
Hua Hong has accelerated investment in its third fab project in Wuxi, in China’s eastern province of Jiangsu. Registered capital at the joint venture managing the fab skyrocketed to US$4.17 billion from 6.68 million yuan (US$998,000) earlier this month – an over 4,000-fold increase – according to Chinese corporate database Tianyancha.
The venture has drawn major state investors, including the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund – known as the “Big Fund” – alongside local government capital.
The move follows a fundraising round in September, when Hua Hong invested US$2 billion in the facility. Hua Hong and its Shanghai subsidiary hold a combined 51 per cent controlling stake, with the remaining stake held by state-backed investors.
Construction of the facility, known as Fab 9B, began in March. It would focus on specialty technology chips used in power devices, analog chips and embedded storage, according to Hua Hong.
Once fully operational, Fab 9B would add 55,000 wafers to Hua Hong’s monthly production capacity, expanding its total Wuxi capacity by roughly 30 per cent.
During an earnings call in May, Hua Hong chairman and president Bai Peng said the company “did not see any impact” from US export controls on equipment procurement for the Wuxi project.
Hua Hong’s Hong Kong-listed shares fell 1.1 per cent to HK$94.55 on Friday, tracking a broader pullback across Chinese semiconductor stocks.

data.title: China’s hotel room rates disappoint during ‘golden week’ despite tourism boom
data.description:
Hotel room rates across mainland China fell short of expectations during the National Day “golden week” holiday despite a tourism boom, as company officials and analysts called for stronger asset and revenue management to ease pricing pressure.
Hotel tariffs remained largely unchanged from the previous month between October 1 and 7, even as bookings jumped, according to executives at hotel operators and travel agencies.
“The days when hotels and resorts could expect a windfall during the week-long holiday are history,” said Li Wenjie, CEO of Shanghai Yaheng International Travel. “Middle-income tourists are no longer willing to spend freely on accommodation.”
The subdued performance stood in stark contrast to the surge in room prices seen three years ago after Beijing lifted its zero-Covid-19 policy. During the 2023 National Day holiday, some hotel operators inflated rates to as much as 10 times their average levels.
Online travel agency Qunar reported ahead of the holiday that hotel bookings in popular tourist destinations on the mainland had risen about 30 per cent year on year.
“New supply, measured corporate travel and outbound tourism are somewhat eroding room rates,” said Zhou Tao, head of hotels and hospitality at JLL in China.
“Operators should adopt total-revenue management, price around events and peak periods, and diversify into local, MICE [meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions] and extended-stay demand.”
Some hotels in China were also burdened by outdated designs that no longer met the needs of today’s travellers, he added.
Leading hospitality groups from Hilton to Shangri-La have been doubling down on lifestyle brands over the past two years to cater to mainland tourists’ growing appetite for personalised and culturally immersive experiences, helping support room rates and occupancy.
Last year, Shangri-La launched its super-luxury hotel brand, Shangri-La Signatures, in China, combining cultural heritage and nature to attract wealthy tourists with unique experiences.
In July, Hilton introduced its Tempo brand to China. Alan Watts, the group’s president for the Asia-Pacific region, said the move would help hotel owners capture growing demand for lifestyle-oriented hospitality through a scalable business model.
Last month, Herman Chui, senior director of office, hotel and residence at Hong Kong developer Hang Lung Properties, said modern hotels should offer guests more personalised experiences, from selecting in-room amenities like teapots to allowing them to bring along their pets.
“Refurbishment should follow a clear target-segment strategy rather than a generic upgrade, with labour, energy and procurement costs aligned to demand,” Zhou of JLL said.
“Professional asset management is required to implement [strategic] repositioning, rebranding and renovation to achieve rejuvenation with better and healthier performance as well as asset value for hotels.”
There are signs of hope for the sector. Analysts said events could generate concentrated, date-specific demand from cross-city visitors, giving venue-adjacent hotels greater pricing power.
As a prime test case, Shanghai will kick off the 25th China Shanghai International Arts Festival (CSIAF) on October 17 to attract visitors from around the globe.
The month-long grand cultural event will feature about 400 programmes and more than 1,100 performances.
Highlights include the Shanghai debut of Dance Reflections by Van Cleef & Arpels, appearances by Grammy Award-winning Chinese composer Tan Dun, and the “Focus on Germany” cultural week showcasing German classical arts.
“The festival will enable Shanghai to truly earn its status as a premier global destination for the performing arts,” said Li Ming, president of the CSIAF. “It will be a festival filled with top-notch artists and performances.”

data.title: Ex-university student jailed for 7 years for rape, sexual assault and voyeurism
data.description:
A Hong Kong court has sentenced a former university student to seven years in prison for raping and sexually targeting five women, with some of the crimes taking place at orientation camps.
The 31-year-old defendant was sentenced on Friday at the High Court after a jury found him guilty of one count of rape, another of voyeurism and three counts of indecent assault. The five convictions concerned offences committed between January and August 2023.
The defendant, identified only by his initials YLH, was a fourth-year student at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdU) in Tai Po at the time.
He denied the allegations, and the victims testified at his trial.
At a joint school orientation camp in July 2023, the defendant was playing a drinking game with a male student, Noah, and another woman in a room.
When Noah left, the defendant took advantage of the woman and groped her several times. He then escalated the assault and raped her that night.

The following month at an EdU camp, the defendant secretly observed a woman showering before pulling open her shower curtain.
At the same camp, he also molested two other women. On one occasion, he approached one of the victims at a campfire and touched her thigh.
Another victim, who was not associated with any of the camps, also said the defendant sexually assaulted her in January that year inside his car after the pair had a drink in Central one night.
The court heard that the defendant offered to drive the victim home, but instead took her to Kowloon Peak – a secluded area – where he molested her when she was unable to escape.
Citing the victim impact reports, Madam Justice Esther Toh Lye-ping said the woman who was raped suffered from moderate depression and anxiety.
Toh handed down a six-year sentence for the offence of rape.
She ordered the defendant to serve a consecutive term of one year and one week for the remaining four charges.

data.title: China holiday travel, pension gains: 5 figures investors are watching in China
data.description:
Hong Kong’s property market showed renewed strength as a Kowloon residential site fetched its highest price in nearly five years, while the city’s pension funds posted solid gains despite a September setback. Meanwhile, global investors returned to Chinese equities after years of caution, as US Treasury yields surged to multi-decade highs.
Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week.
China records 2.14 billion passenger trips over National Day holiday
China recorded 2.14 billion cross-regional passenger trips during the seven-day National Day holiday, averaging 306 million journeys a day, up 0.7 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Transport.
The holiday box office fell 36.5 per cent to 1.165 billion yuan from a year earlier, according to National Film Administration data reported by CCTV, though this year’s holiday was one day shorter than last year’s.
US 10-year Treasury yield hits 24-year high of 5.36 per cent
The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.36 per cent on Wednesday, its highest level in 24 years, as rising oil prices and persistent inflation concerns triggered another sell-off in government bonds.
The 30-year yield also reached a 24-year high of 5.7 per cent, although a strong US$39 billion auction of 10-year notes later helped ease selling pressure, suggesting that higher yields were attracting investors back into the market.


Hong Kong’s MPF gains nearly HK$100 billion in first nine months
Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund generated HK$96.9 billion (US$12.34 billion) in investment gains over the first nine months of the year, delivering an average return of 6.2 per cent, according to MPF Ratings on Wednesday.
The gains came despite a setback in September, when the city’s compulsory retirement scheme lost HK$25.1 billion, or 1.47 per cent, across its 382 investment funds.
Global funds end four-year underweight stance on Chinese equities
Global active long-only funds have raised their allocations to Chinese equities to benchmark-neutral levels, ending four years of underweight positioning, according to Bank of America.
The shift, observed across nearly 2,800 funds managing US$562 billion in Chinese stocks, reflects renewed interest in relatively cheap valuations and artificial intelligence opportunities, although analysts cautioned that it did not necessarily signal a bullish turn.
Kerry Properties pays HK$4.31 billion for Kowloon residential site
Kerry Properties acquired a residential plot in Ho Man Tin for HK$4.31 billion (US$549 million), according to Hong Kong’s Lands Department on Tuesday, the highest price paid for a residential site in Kowloon in nearly five years.
The Fat Kwong Street site fetched HK$20,738 per square foot of gross floor area, reflecting developers’ renewed appetite for prime residential land amid expectations of resilient demand for luxury homes.
